abstract_text: Sharks, rays, and chimaeras (hereafter ‘sharks’) are often overlooked in spatial planning for biodiversity conservation. The Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA) project, launched by the IUCN Species Survival Commission Shark Specialist Group in 2022, provides a tool to address this globally. The initiative identifies three-dimensional portions of habitat that are important for one or more shark species and have the potential to be managed for conservation. A set of science-based criteria are used to delineate these areas and consider species vulnerability, range restriction, life-history (reproduction, feeding, resting, movement, undefined aggregations), and special attributes (distinctiveness, diversity). These criteria are being applied to all environments where sharks occur across 13 ISRA regions covering the entire globe. Collaboration is paramount with experts convening at regional workshops to share information and propose important areas. Sixty five ISRAs have been delineated in the Central and South American Pacific and 75 proposals are undergoing review for the Mediterranean and Black Seas. Areas are also currently being evaluated for the Western Indian Ocean and other regions will follow. Peer-reviewed and approved ISRAs are mapped and added to a publicly available eAtlas (www.sharkrayareas.org). By centralising key information on shark habitat use and behaviour, ISRAs provide a foundation to ensure sharks are included in area-based management. This assists governments and policymakers in meeting global biodiversity and conservation targets, especially when such areas are overlapped with other approaches such as Important Marine Mammal Areas (IMMAs). Results from the ISRA initiative will support shark conservation by increasing information available when considering spatial management of these highly threatened species.

abstract_text: Large sharks are important predators in marine ecosystems, influencing the overall functioning of ecosystems and the trophic connectivity between different regions (Heithaus et al., 2008; Estes et al., 2011). However, they face intense fishing pressure, particularly in coastal areas that serve as nurseries for many juvenile sharks (Fowler et al., 2005; Heupel et al., 2007). Understanding the spatial and temporal ecology of sharks in interaction with fisheries, especially in coastal ecosystems such as estuaries and lagoons, is crucial for their conservation. Many shark species, including Sphyrna lewini (scalloped hammerhead shark) and Carcharhinus limbatus (blacktip shark), are considered threatened with extinction (Dulvy et al., 2014). Recent observations in artisanal fishing in Gabon have revealed an abundance of juvenile sharks belonging to these two species, suggesting the presence of undocumented nurseries. The southern coast of Gabon, with its lagoon complexes and mangrove habitats, could play a key role in maintaining shark populations in the equatorial Atlantic (Cadenat et al., 1955; Mourier et al., 2013). This study aims to demonstrate the existence of nurseries for Sphyrna lewini and Carcharhinus limbatus in Gabon by studying captures, the maturity of captured individuals, and their trophic ecology.

abstract_text: Over one third of elasmobranch species are threatened with extinction with nearly all species impacted by fisheries, typically from bycatch. While much research has been conducted on the impacts of certain threats on elasmobranchs, i.e., fishing, climate, discarding, and finning, there is a gap in the knowledge of how elasmobranch distributions might respond to population decline as a result of these threats. Furthermore, not all species will recover at the same rate, as some species are intrinsically more sensitive than others. Our goal was to determine the sensitivity of local elasmobranch species and highlight areas where these species and threats consistently overlap. Here we have determined the biological sensitivity of 44 species of elasmobranch found in Irish waters using the metric rmax, the maximum intrinsic rate of population increase. Oviparous species were found to have higher rmax than than ovoviviparous species in general, and the deep sea species had the lowest rmax, determining these species to be the most sensitive. Next we applied a species distribution modelling (SDM) approach to predict the distribution of 3 sensitive elasmobranch species found in Irish waters, as determined by rmax. Projections identified a change in the spatial distribution and extent of several species, with the results used to identify potential ‘hotspots’ of sensitive elasmobranchs in Irish waters based on intrinsic and extrinsic factors. Outputs of this work will help to improve the understanding of the local variability of elasmobranch species and provide support to expand and improve the management of protected areas and species.

abstract_text: Skates (Rajidae) are important commercial species around the British Isles, yet there is currently limited information to aid the identification of potentially important habitats, such as spawning and nursery grounds. The neonates and juveniles of skate species have been recorded in scientific trawl surveys, with juveniles of most species proportionally more frequent in beam trawl surveys than in otter trawl surveys. The Great Eggcase Hunt is a long-standing (2003 to present) citizen science recording project that collates georeferenced data for elasmobranch eggcases, primarily from around the British Isles. This provided verified species-specific data for a total of 227,407 specimens from 11 skate species. Purse Search Ireland provided a further 2,491 records of 10 skate species. Eggcases from the genus Raja were the most frequently observed skate eggcases from much of the British coastline, and juveniles were captured in inshore waters of England and Wales. The juveniles of Raja microocellata were most common in shallow water, and the limited data available for R. undulata also indicates that any nursery grounds for this species would also be in shallow water. Juveniles of the genus Leucoraja occurred further offshore, although only the eggcases of L. naevus were recorded regularly on trawl surveys (with an L. fullonica eggcase recorded just once). The earliest free-living stages also occurred offshore. An improved knowledge of spawning and nursery grounds can be used to aid fisheries management and marine spatial planning, and may also inform the emerging interest in Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs).

abstract_text: All elasmobranchs are fully protected from fishing practices in Israel. In this ‘safe haven’, research led by the Morris Kahn Marine Research Station’s Marine Apex Predator Laboratory has shown that dusky sharks (Carcharhinus obscurus) and sandbar sharks (C. plumbeus) return to aggregate in the winter months (November-May) along the Israeli coastline (1-20 m depth; est. 80-100 individuals). We expect that they inhabit these areas due to the warm water discharge relative to the ambient winter temperatures (22-25°C from the power plant; ambient 16-18°C). Ours is the only long-term catch-and-release programme in the Mediterranean Basin. Currently, both species belong to Annex III of the Barcelona Convention and are evaluated as ‘Data Deficient and ‘Endangered’ on the IUCN Mediterranean Red List, respectively. Female sandbar sharks are increasingly observed with each tagging season in Israel and since 2018, we have proof that the dusky sharks are inhabiting this space during some stage of their gestation, yet we still do not know where their parturition grounds are. To answer this, we collaborated with Dr James Sulikowski, leading expert of shark reproductive biology, and co-developer of the innovative Birth-Alert Tag with Lotek Wireless. With funding from National Geographic, this state-of-the-art intrauterine satellite tag was deployed in one gravid dusky shark in April 2023 after confirmation of pregnancy via ultrasonogram, with further samples taken for physiological analyses. Further detections of this shark via acoustic transmitter were made until late May, which is unusual for this species. We present this suite of information relating to non-invasive methods.

abstract_text: Distribution of species across regulatory and physical boundaries poses a recognised challenge to effective management and research, and these transboundary species tend to suffer more-severe population declines. Large pelagic sharks like the porbeagle, Lamna nasus, are particularly vulnerable due to their life history characteristics including their highly migratory behaviour, whereby the latter is particularly challenging for management in European waters where management jurisdictions change over small spatial scales. We used high-resolution satellite tags to demonstrate that individual porbeagles in the region display high inter-individual variation in behaviour, undertaking very rapid movements (up to 100 km per day) through multiple EEZs and physical habitats, transiting different management zones in a matter of days along different paths. These data highlight the value of existing and the urgent need for continued regional collaboration and cross-border funding mechanisms to maximise research impact to fill knowledge gaps and improve conservation outcomes for vulnerable and highly mobile shark species.

abstract_text: Identifying the timing of key life history events, such as mating, is important for conserving endangered species. Yet, for many elasmobranchs, there is a paucity of data on reproductive timings. Developing low-cost and non-invasive methods for estimating elasmobranch reproductive timings could assist in closing the knowledge gap and aid collecting reproductive information on more species. The flapper skate (Dipturus intermedius) is a critically endangered elasmobranch and the largest skate found in European waters. A large flapper skate photo-ID database exists, featuring photographs taken throughout the year provided by members of the public. Here, we present novel work making opportunistic use of the flapper skate photo-ID database to estimate flapper skate reproductive timing. A methodology was developed to identify the occurrence of three indicators of reproductive activity visible in photographs: pelvic swelling, bite wounds, and scratch wounds. Over 2000 images were examined for presence of each indicator and the seasonality of their occurrence was analysed via generalised additive models. Results suggest flapper skate mate over winter and lay eggs in winter and spring. The findings are corroborated by existing literature, supporting the approach as a valid method for estimating elasmobranch reproductive timing. The developed approach for analysing images could be applied to other species and make use of citizen science, providing another route for understanding reproduction in elusive elasmobranchs.

abstract_text: A huge gap in environmental information exists in conflict regions where access to scientists ranges from unsafe to impossible. Previously unknown knowledge of Elasmobranchii presence, composition, and distribution can provide valuable fisheries information regarding the exploitation of elasmobranch species and for creating comprehensive conservation strategies. However, the diversity, ecology, behavior, and many other characteristics of these species in conflict zones remain virtually unknown, which is a major cause for concern. Traditional species assessments rely on in-situ observations, market surveys, and regulatory authorities forcing fisheries to self-report their catch. Conflict areas present a unique challenge, lacking formal regulation or scientific access. Here, we report the first use of social media monitoring for the extent of the Elasmobranch fishery in the Gaza Strip (east Mediterranean), a conflict region previously lacking any information. Our database consists of 3 years of daily reported catch from 16 fish stores and social media fishery-related influencers in the Gaza Strip. We collected 1530 data points belonging to 4619 individuals of 20 species. The analysis of the data sheds light on previously unknown temporal, spatial, and seasonal trends in elasmobranch catch distribution and relations to changes in the access to maritime areas due to local conflict escalations. We demonstrate this approach as a relatively accurate and inexpensive data mining procedure, allowing the quantification and normalization of multiple observations of caught and targeted fish into a uniformed geo-spatial-temporal system- making it a prime candidate for future endeavors in other data-poor regions and conflict zones in coastal areas.

abstract_text: The environment sector, including organisations working to protect the marine environment, is the second-least diverse in the UK. There is an urgent need to address barriers to participation and diversify opportunities for involvement in conservation and research, as the marine environment has a vital role in natural, cultural, social and economic heritage for all communities. Project SIARC (Sharks Inspiring Action and Research with Communities) uses flagship elasmobranchs in Wales (angelshark, blue skate, common stingray, flapper skate, spurdog, and tope) to bring together local communities, fishers, researchers and government to cultivate a new appreciation and open-up access to the underwater environment in Wales. A major part of our work is to identify approaches that enable a wider range of people to engage with marine conservation in Wales and tackle the lack of diversity and inclusion within Project SIARC, thereby contributing to wider systemic change. abstract_text: Large urban and industrial settlements, and the intense maritime traffic make the Mediterranean one of the most polluted areas in the world. This basin hosts considerable marine biodiversity, including many elasmobranchs, which are extremely vulnerable to environmental contamination due their life history traits. The impact of this threat on the cartilaginous fishes is still poorly studied, as well as the possible consequences for human health, in case of consumption of sharks, are uncertain. To fill this knowledge gap, quantitative and qualitative assessments of three groups of persistent organic pollutants (POPs) were carried out in the muscle and liver of two shark species, Mustelus punctulatus and Mustelus mustelus, caught in the Marine Protected Area (MPA) of Egadi Islands (South-Central Mediterranean Sea) between 2021 and 2023. As sharks are one of the top predators inhabiting the MPA, they can be considered a bioindicator of the local environmental status. Paradoxically, although M. punctulatus and M. mustelus have considerable commercial value for human consumption in the MPA, they are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN in the Mediterranean. Regarding POPs levels, the results showed a trend of PCBs > DDTs >> HCB in liver and muscle for both species. Our results can significantly contribute to clarify the toxicological status of these species, allowing a first evaluation of the real risks both for the local marine life and for human health.

abstract_text: Very little is known about the biology and ecology of the nursehound shark Scyliorhinus stellaris (Linnaeus, 1758), a medium-sized catshark in severe decline in the Mediterranean Sea, assessed as Near Threatened (Vulnerable in the Atlantic) by the IUCN. This ongoing citizen science project provides insights on basic reproductive information on this species in the wild, such as: seasonality, development, predation and natural mortality rates, and indications that this nursery area is in decline. Photo-identification reveals that this area is also a resting area for adults of both sexes, which is used year-round and over multiple years. This nursery area is a no-fishing zone and falls within a Natura 2000 site. In spite of its protected status, illegal fishing occurs as the whole Gulf is subject to intense artisanal and recreational fishing pressure. Results of the Stellaris project allowed the Santa Croce Bank to be identified by the IUCN as an ISRA, an Important Shark and Ray Area, highlighting the importance of this refuge and the need for increased management and conservation actions for this neglected species. These results also highlight the value of citizen science in making tangible conservation contribution.

abstract_text: Sharks and rays in the Red Sea region are under intense fishing pressure, heavy development, and extensive tourism load. The IUCN report on the status of sharks and rays in the Arabian Sea and adjacent waters from 2017 found that at least half of the species are endangered. Based on these species assessments, in the Red Sea alone the number of endangered species is alarmingly higher, presenting a state of danger to almost all cartilaginous fish species that live in it. We have established a citizen science project SRS (sharks and rays in the Red Sea), based on the MECO Protocol, collecting observations from the public through social networks with the aim of gathering up-to-date basic biological and ecological information. abstract_text: Spurdog (Squalus acanthias), otherwise known as Spiny or Picked Dogfish, are members of the dogfish (Squalidae) family. They are distinguished by the presence of a spine in front of each dorsal fin. They have a wide distribution, mainly inhabiting temperate waters. This species was originally listed on the IUCN Red List as Critically Endangered, but through a non-genuine change in 2015, Spurdog was changed to Endangered in Europe (IUCN, 2015). In the Northeast Atlantic, there has been a fishery for Spurdog since the early 20th century. This population was overexploited which led to population decline. Various management measures have been put in place to aid recovery of this population, including placing Spurdog on the Prohibited species list. In 2022, ICES gave advice that the population could support a fishery for 2023 and 2024. In 2023, the fishery was reopened with a TAC of 17,353 tonnes (t) across the region. The UK has a quota of 4,825 t in Western waters and 2,781 t in the North Sea. As of October 2023, 194.0 t (4.0%) and 95.0 t (4.6%) of these quotas have been landed respectively. This presentation discusses the management history of Spurdog and the possible dangers of reopening a fishery on tentative signs of recovery.

abstract_text: The spurdog (Squalus acanthias Linnaeus, 1758) Northeast Atlantic stock is managed as a single unit and has undergone a long period of overfishing, especially in the 1950s/1960s, which has caused its population to collapse. There are now signs of population growth but it remains listed as “Endangered” and overexploitation may have had an impact on its genetic composition. Limited data are available on the stocks genetic structure and properly delineating a stock unit for fisheries management is crucial to allow sustainability of the exploited population. Population genetics provides valuable insights into connectivity and genetic distinctions among individuals from different areas. Looking at genetic diversity within and between populations is also important in terms of population resilience in the face of climate change or other pressures such as overexploitation. A first assessment of the population structure was done using the NADH dehydrogenase subunit 2 (ND2) mitochondrial marker sequenced from 48 spurdogs sampled along the Norwegian part of the Northeast Atlantic. 25 unique haplotypes were distinguished, showing high genetic diversity in Norwegian waters, but no genetic distinction between sampling locations. To provide more accurate population level data, over 89 individuals from identical locations were used for genome-wide analysis, involving 53492 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) derived from Restriction-site associated DNA sequencing (RAD-seq). Clustering analysis revealed subpopulations along Norwegian waters. This study presents this population structure and discusses their relevance for regional fishery management purposes.

abstract_text: In the ocean, mobile species exhibit diverse movements across different spatial and temporal scales. Understanding the drivers behind these movements is essential for effective management and predicting responses to a changing ocean environment. A multitude of environmental cues, such as temperature and salinity, have been shown to affect the movements of elasmobranch species. However, it is increasingly recognized that social drivers may also influence movement. We conducted an acoustic telemetry study in a partially enclosed sea loch on the west coast of Scotland to investigate the movements and habitat selection of spurdog (Squalus acanthias). Spurdog segregate based on size and sex, and these subgroups display a high range of movements, from transatlantic movements to coastal residency. Some subgroups also display high levels of relatedness, suggesting kinship bonds within subgroups. Our findings revealed that spurdog exhibited a high level of year-round residency within the loch and that temperature plays a pivotal role in their habitat selection. Additionally, subgroups within the population display different habitat choices, which may be caused by underlying population social processes. This study underscores the importance of understanding all drivers of animal movement. Identifying sites that promote residential behaviour can aid in developing effective management strategies for species, like the spurdog. However, it is equally crucial to comprehend the social drivers of movement, as they can significantly influence habitat choices. By considering the interplay between environmental and social factors, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of animal movements and enhance conservation efforts for these mobile ocean species.

abstract_text: Mobile sharks are more at risk of encountering human activities such as fisheries, putting high bycatch pressure on shark populations. Spurdog (Squalus acanthias) was historically exploited by a well-documented fishery, however, relatively little is known about their large-scale movements, habitat preferences, and population dynamics after the stock collapse in the late 1990s. abstract_text: Effective conservation measures are urgently needed for elasmobranchs. People possess significant power in driving conservation efforts, but elasmobranchs, known for historically evoking irrational attitudes, have been overlooked. abstract_text: Establishing how threatened wildlife are distributed spatially and temporally is essential for effective conservation and management planning. abstract_text: Skates (Rajiformes) represent one of the most intriguing cases of high species richness coupled with extremely conservative morphological and ecological traits. Small differences are described within and between species and increasing cases of cryptic speciation have been recorded among sister and non-sister taxa. More interestingly, this condition has been frequently observed in Central Atlantic Ocean (CAO), along the coasts of Western Africa, between Angola and Senegal, where oceanographic heterogeneities such as current systems, may play a key role for ecological speciation in skates. The use of multiple mtDNA loci and its integration with nuDNA microsatellite has been successfully applied to estimate the genetic variation in skate species inhabiting the CAO. Phylogenetic reconstructions, phylogeographic patterns and genetic connectivity estimates were applied to test the hypothesis that restricted gene flow and genetic divergence within Raja species reflect known climate and bio-oceanographic discontinuities. The widely distributed Raja miraletus species complex counts five deeply distinct lineages three of which co-occur in CAO: the Angolan Raja cf. miraletus, the Senegalese and sympatric R. parva and Raja cf. miraletus. In addition, an ancient, hidden lineage nesting in the clade Raja straeleni/R. clavata/R. maderensis was identified in Angola. The complexity of oceanographic system acting in the CAO (i.e., the Benguela Current region and the intertropical Canary current inflowing from the northeast) may have influenced the diversification of the Angolan and Senegalese taxa, boosting the biodiversity of the area, in an unprecedented anthology of species-specific evolutionary histories.

abstract_text: Microplastics (plastic particles sized under 5mm) are ubiquitous in the marine environment. They are known to have negative effects on marine organisms when ingested, including accumulation in digestive systems, causing starvation, and leaching of toxic chemicals, impacting development and reproduction. The habitat of reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi), a filter-feeding elasmobranch, overlaps with plastic pollution hotspots globally. This makes them at risk of ingesting the particles, with potential negative consequences on their fitness. The species is already listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red list, due to other anthropogenic pressures, such as fishing. It is therefore important to understand the risk of plastic pollution on this charismatic megafaunal species. This study is investigating the presence of microplastics in reef manta ray feeding grounds in the Chagos Archipelago. This is a no-take Marine Protected Area, home to a resident population of reef manta rays. However remote, the beaches of the Archipelago are covered in plastic debris which originates from elsewhere. This suggests there will be plenty of microplastics in the Archipelago waters. Quantifying the amount of microplastic in the water will build a better picture of how it could impact the local population of reef manta rays. It will also hopefully input into wider conversations about plastic reduction on remote islands.

abstract_text: Environmental temperature affects physiological functions, representing a barrier for the range expansions of ectothermic species. To understand the link between thermal physiology and biogeography, a key question is whether among-species thermal sensitivity of metabolic rates is mechanistically constrained or buffered through physiological remodeling over evolutionary time. The former conception, the Universal Temperature Dependence hypothesis, predicts similar among- and within-species thermal sensitivity. The latter conception, the Metabolic Cold Adaptation hypothesis, predicts lower among-species thermal sensitivity than within-species sensitivity. Previous studies that tested these hypotheses for fishes overwhelmingly investigated teleosts with elasmobranchs understudied. Here, we show that among-species thermal sensitivity of resting metabolic rates is lower than within-species sensitivity in teleosts but not in elasmobranchs. Further, species richness declines with latitude more rapidly in elasmobranchs than in teleosts. Metabolic Cold Adaptation exhibited by teleosts might underpin their high diversity at high latitudes, whereas the inflexible thermal sensitivity approximated by Universal Temperature Dependence of elasmobranchs might explain their low diversity at high latitudes. These findings are discussed in the context of range expansions of sharks and rays, including recent examples from Ireland and the UK.

abstract_text: One of the chief consequences of climate change is the worldwide redistribution of species in the pursue of physiologically and ecologically favourable conditions. Sharks have been described as the aquatic ‘big game’ equivalent, displayed as ‘trophies’ and caught for the ‘thrill of the fight’. Historical fears of sharks have led to an increase in shark fishing tournaments, increasing the rate of decline of shark populations threatened with extinction. However, modern-day social science studies in the United States and Australia have contradicted these fears, with a growing desire amongst anglers to become advocates for shark conservation. Here, we examine anglers’ motivations behind shark fishing in the United Kingdom (UK) a popular but understudied location for recreational shark fishing. Angler demographics, perceptions towards sharks and perceptions of shark population trends were also explored. A total of seven shark fishing operators and 44 recreational anglers responded to our structured surveys throughout Aug-Nov 2021. Respondents primarily comprised of over-fifty, educated and wealthy male anglers. Anglers were motivated by the ‘appreciation for sharks and nature’ (n=43) and the ‘thrill/challenge’ (n=38). Obtaining a photo (status) was the least popular reason for taking part in shark fishing, further contradicting historical studies. Recreational shark fishing in the UK is strictly catch and release, with anglers demonstrating best practice techniques to minimise stress to caught sharks. abstract_text: Most elasmobranch populations are under pressure, and to advise policy makers on appropriate conservation measures, data on abundance, life history traits, spawning grounds and population structure are required. The application of DNA based techniques can provide some of this information, but commonly is dependent on tissue sampling (e.g., muscle, scale and blood) which requires handling and potentially underestimate less common species. Environmental DNA (eDNA) is shown as a reliable tool for the assessment of elasmobranch species diversity, but so far is unable to provide reliable data on population diversity. Egg cases of oviparous elasmobranchs can form a valuable aid in determining a species spatial distribution, defining spawning areas and DNA based analysis of population structure. So far, egg cases for this type of research were collected from both commercial fisheries and scientific surveys, generally with the embryo still inside, ensuring the quality of DNA. However, many of the egg cases wash up on shore after hatching departure or predation. When exposed to the elements, the genetic material in the egg case will start degrading, but DNA fragments of sufficient quality could still be viable for population genetics. We now present the successful isolation and sequencing of 2kb long mtDNA fragments from 14-day-old, hatched egg cases using a combination of liquid nitrogen, keratinase and collagenase. Developing this method further, beached egg cases collected by means of citizen science can provide a useful tool to determine oviparous elasmobranch population structure with limited resources and the added bonus of creating public awareness.

abstract_text: To achieve sustainable shark fisheries, it is as important to understand the social and economic drivers of overfishing as it is the biological drivers and environmental consequences. The extinction risk of sharks is disproportionately higher in coastal tropical waters where small-scale fisheries dominate, presenting unique management challenges. Small-scale fisheries provide a critical source of economic and nutritional security, but fishers are among the most vulnerable socio-economic groups because their exposure to economic, social, and environmental shocks is combined with limited adaptive capacity. Using Kenya and Zanzibar as a case study, we examine the interactions between sharks and small-scale fisheries. We find that sharks are an important source of economic and nutritional security, primarily from species threatened with extinction. Further, the most economically valuable sharks are larger, slower reproducing, and more likely to be threatened with extinction, providing a strong economic incentive to target endangered species. Given the high economic motivation and intensive fishing pressure, small-scale fisheries are undoubtedly important contributors to the ongoing decline of many threatened shark species. The decline of sharks may have damaging consequences for wider marine ecosystems and ecosystem services. In the absence of effective fisheries management, we show that within small-scale fisheries the conditions exist for an economically incentivised positive feedback loop in which vulnerable fishers are driven to persistently overfish vulnerable and declining resources. In doing so, they undermine their own economic and nutritional security and that of their communities. To be successful management must break the feedback loop or be doomed to failure.
